triage.name: Congenital hypothyroidism
triage.reason: Infant with prolonged jaundice, constipation, poor feeding and hypotonia; classically detected on newborn screening, and a treatable cause of developmental delay.

review_issues: presentation: term 'Abnormal newborn screening test' not found in SNOMED CT

presentation: term 'Poor growth' not found in SNOMED CT

exam: term 'Delayed relaxation of deep tendon reflex' not found in SNOMED CT

demographics: Occurs in about 1 in 2,000 to 4,000 newborns; female infants are affected about twice as often as males
Most common in regions with iodine deficiency, though in the US it is usually sporadic and not iodine-related
More common in infants with Down syndrome and other congenital syndromes

risk_factors.text: Family history of thyroid disease or congenital hypothyroidism
Maternal iodine deficiency or exposure to antithyroid drugs, radioactive iodine, or amiodarone during pregnancy
Consanguinity or known genetic syndromes affecting thyroid development

family_history: Thyroid disease in a parent or sibling
exposures: Maternal antithyroid medication (methimazole, propylthiouracil) during pregnancy
Iodine deficiency or excess iodine exposure

chief_complaints.text: My baby is very sleepy and hard to feed
My baby has been constipated since birth
The newborn screening test was abnormal
My baby's skin looks yellow and puffy

hpi.onset: Insidious, present from birth or within the first few weeks of life
hpi.duration: Weeks to months if not detected on newborn screening
hpi.progression: Gradual worsening of feeding, activity, and growth; symptoms may be subtle at first and become more obvious over the first months
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate at birth, progressive if untreated
pertinent_negatives: Failure to pass meconium in the first 48 hours

atypical.how_it_differs: Many infants are asymptomatic at birth because maternal thyroid hormone crosses the placenta; signs appear gradually over the first weeks to months.
If not detected and treated early, older infants and children present with severe growth failure, developmental delay, and coarse facial features.

general.mild: Alert but sleepy, feeds slowly, mild hypotonia
general.moderate: Lethargic, poor feeding, hypotonia, puffy face, hoarse cry
general.severe: Markedly lethargic, weak cry, marked hypotonia, coarse facial features, macroglossia, umbilical hernia
general.critical: Lethargic to obtunded, poor respiratory effort, bradycardia, hypothermia, myxedema

findings.finding: Wide open anterior fontanelle with delayed closure

findings.maneuver: Inspect the oral cavity and tongue
findings.finding: Enlarged tongue protruding from the mouth
Coarse facial features with puffy eyelids and broad flat nose

findings.maneuver: Inspect the eyes and periorbital area
Inspect the skin and sclerae in natural light
findings.finding: Yellow discoloration of skin and sclerae (prolonged jaundice)

findings.maneuver: Palpate the skin of the face and extremities
Inspect the umbilicus and palpate the abdominal wall

findings.finding: Mild abdominal distension due to constipation

findings.maneuver: Assess muscle tone by passive range of motion and traction
findings.finding: Decreased resistance to passive movement, floppy posture

findings.maneuver: Elicit deep tendon reflexes (e.g., knee jerk)
findings.finding: Prolonged relaxation phase of the reflex
findings.term: Delayed relaxation of deep tendon reflex

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the heart and palpate the pulse
findings.finding: Heart rate below normal for age
Cardiac murmur suggesting associated congenital heart defect
Clear breath sounds without crackles or wheezing

findings.maneuver: Perform a neurologic exam including cranial nerves and motor function
findings.finding: No focal neurologic deficits or seizures

labs.caveat: Elevated TSH is the key screening and confirmatory finding. In central (secondary/tertiary) hypothyroidism TSH is low or inappropriately normal, so a normal TSH does not exclude the diagnosis when free T4 is low.
Low free T4 confirms the diagnosis. In central hypothyroidism free T4 is low with a low or normal TSH.
Unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia from prolonged physiologic jaundice; helps explain the presenting jaundice.
Direct fraction is low, confirming the jaundice is unconjugated.
Mild anemia is common in untreated hypothyroidism and resolves with replacement.
Hyponatremia can occur in severe untreated hypothyroidism; check if the infant is lethargic or seizing.
Hypoglycemia is uncommon but can occur in the severely hypothyroid neonate.

imaging.preferred_when: First-line imaging to determine whether a thyroid gland is present and where it is located

findings.text: Absent thyroid tissue in the normal pretracheal location (athyreosis)
Ectopic thyroid tissue along the thyroglossal duct path, often at the base of the tongue
Normal-sized or enlarged gland in the normal location (dyshormonogenesis or transient causes)

imaging.preferred_when: When ultrasound is inconclusive or to confirm ectopic tissue and quantify functioning thyroid tissue

findings.text: No uptake in the thyroid bed (athyreosis)
Uptake in an ectopic location such as the tongue base
Normal or increased uptake in a eutopic gland (dyshormonogenesis)

imaging.study: Left hand and wrist radiograph for bone age
imaging.preferred_when: To assess the severity and duration of in-utero hypothyroidism

findings.text: Delayed bone age with absent or small distal femoral and proximal tibial epiphyses

imaging.preferred_when: Only if a murmur or signs of congenital heart disease are present

findings.text: Associated congenital heart defect such as a septal defect

initial.why: Primary test for congenital hypothyroidism; elevated in primary disease
Confirms low thyroid hormone and distinguishes primary from central hypothyroidism
Assesses for anemia and provides a baseline before starting therapy
Evaluates electrolytes, glucose, and renal function in a lethargic infant
Determines whether the gland is absent, ectopic, or in place

supporting.why: Localizes ectopic tissue or confirms athyreosis when ultrasound is inconclusive
supporting.only_if: ultrasound is inconclusive or ectopic tissue is suspected

supporting.test: Left hand and wrist radiograph for bone age
supporting.why: Documents delayed skeletal maturation and severity of prenatal hypothyroidism
supporting.only_if: the diagnosis is confirmed and severity assessment is needed

supporting.why: Explains prolonged jaundice and excludes other causes of neonatal hyperbilirubinemia

not_indicated.why: Not routine; reserve for a murmur or suspected congenital heart defect
not_indicated.only_if: a murmur or signs of congenital heart disease are present

not_indicated.why: No role in the diagnosis of congenital hypothyroidism
Used for Graves disease, not congenital hypothyroidism

decision_points: Any infant with an abnormal newborn screen must have confirmatory serum TSH and free T4 drawn promptly; treatment should not be delayed while awaiting imaging.
Start levothyroxine as soon as the diagnosis is confirmed, ideally within the first two weeks of life, to protect neurodevelopment.
Distinguish primary (high TSH, low free T4) from central (low or normal TSH, low free T4) hypothyroidism before deciding on imaging.
Thyroid imaging is used to determine the cause (dysgenesis versus dyshormonogenesis) but should not delay treatment.

criteria.name: Newborn screening and confirmatory testing
criteria.summary: All newborns in the US are screened with a heel-stick TSH or T4 measurement. An abnormal screen is confirmed with a venous serum TSH and free T4. Primary congenital hypothyroidism is diagnosed when TSH is elevated and free T4 is low; central hypothyroidism is diagnosed when free T4 is low with a low or inappropriately normal TSH.

differential.name: Transient hypothyroidism of prematurity or iodine exposure
differential.why_considered: An abnormal newborn screen with elevated TSH and low free T4 in a preterm or iodine-exposed infant can mimic congenital hypothyroidism.

history: Prematurity or very low birth weight
Maternal or neonatal iodine exposure (povidone-iodine, contrast)
Maternal antithyroid drug use that resolves after drug clearance
exam: Growth and tone improve as the infant matures
labs: TSH and free T4 normalize on repeat testing over weeks
Thyroid autoantibodies may be present but transient
imaging: Thyroid gland present in the normal location on ultrasound

differential.name: Central (secondary or tertiary) hypothyroidism
differential.why_considered: Low free T4 with a low or inappropriately normal TSH can present with the same lethargy, poor feeding, and jaundice as primary congenital hypothyroidism.
differential.trigger: Low free T4 with a low or normal TSH on confirmatory testing

history: May have other pituitary hormone deficiencies
History of birth trauma, hypoxia, or midline defects
exam: Signs of adrenal insufficiency such as hypotension
labs: Low free T4 with low or inappropriately normal TSH
Low cortisol or other pituitary hormone deficiencies
imaging: MRI brain showing pituitary or hypothalamic abnormality

differential.name: Hypothyroidism due to maternal thyroid disease or antibodies
differential.why_considered: Transplacental maternal antithyroid antibodies or antithyroid drugs can cause transient neonatal hypothyroidism with an abnormal screen.

history: Mother with Graves disease, Hashimoto thyroiditis, or on antithyroid medication
Maternal thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin or blocking antibodies
labs: TSH and free T4 normalize after maternal antibodies clear

differential.name: Congenital hypopituitarism
differential.why_considered: Presents with lethargy, poor feeding, hypoglycemia, and jaundice, and can include central hypothyroidism.
differential.trigger: Hypoglycemia, micropenis, or midline defects in a lethargic infant

labs: Low free T4 with low or normal TSH
Low cortisol, low growth hormone, or other pituitary deficiencies
imaging: MRI showing pituitary hypoplasia or ectopic posterior pituitary

differential.name: Benign neonatal prolonged jaundice (breast milk jaundice)
differential.why_considered: Prolonged unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia in a well-appearing breastfed infant can be mistaken for the jaundice of hypothyroidism.

history: Exclusively breastfed and gaining weight well
No constipation, lethargy, or cold intolerance
exam: No puffy face, macroglossia, or umbilical hernia

differential.name: Down syndrome
differential.why_considered: Infants with Down syndrome can have hypotonia, poor feeding, constipation, and an increased risk of congenital hypothyroidism.

history: Characteristic dysmorphic features noted at birth
exam: Upslanting palpebral fissures, single palmar crease, sandal gap
labs: Thyroid function tests may be normal or abnormal

differential.name: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia
differential.why_considered: Can present with lethargy, poor feeding, vomiting, and hypoglycemia in the newborn period.
differential.trigger: Vomiting, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, or ambiguous genitalia in a lethargic infant

severity.mild: Mildly elevated TSH with low-normal free T4; infant is alert, feeding well, with minimal or no classic signs; often detected only on newborn screening.
severity.moderate: Markedly elevated TSH and low free T4; lethargy, poor feeding, constipation, prolonged jaundice, hypotonia, and puffy face are present.
severity.severe: Very high TSH and very low free T4; marked lethargy, weak cry, macroglossia, coarse facial features, umbilical hernia, bradycardia, and hypothermia.
severity.critical: Untreated severe hypothyroidism with myxedema, obtundation, hypothermia, bradycardia, hypoventilation, and hemodynamic instability; rare but life-threatening.

red_flags.finding: Lethargy with poor feeding and failure to thrive
red_flags.meaning: Severe hypothyroidism; needs urgent treatment and evaluation for other causes
Severe hypothyroidism with risk of myxedema; urgent thyroid hormone replacement

red_flags.finding: Hypotonia with weak cry and respiratory difficulty
red_flags.meaning: Severe hypothyroidism or another neuromuscular disorder; assess airway and breathing
Suggests hypothyroidism or other metabolic disease; check thyroid function

red_flags.finding: Umbilical hernia with constipation and macroglossia
red_flags.meaning: Classic severe congenital hypothyroidism; start treatment promptly

complications.name: Irreversible neurodevelopmental impairment
clues: Delayed treatment beyond the first weeks of life

complications.name: Growth failure and short stature
clues: Poor weight gain and linear growth

special_populations.differences: Most newborns are asymptomatic at birth because maternal thyroid hormone crosses the placenta; signs appear gradually over the first weeks to months. Early treatment is critical to prevent neurodevelopmental impairment.
If not detected and treated early, older infants and children present with severe growth failure, developmental delay, and coarse facial features.
Maternal hypothyroidism during pregnancy can affect fetal neurodevelopment; ensure adequate maternal thyroid hormone replacement.

key_questions.question: Was the newborn screening test abnormal, and has it been repeated with a confirmatory serum test?
key_questions.looking_for: An abnormal newborn screen with elevated TSH and low free T4 on confirmatory venous testing

key_questions.question: How is the baby feeding, and how alert is the baby?
key_questions.looking_for: Poor feeding, slow feeding, excessive sleepiness, and lethargy

key_questions.question: How often does the baby have bowel movements, and has constipation been present since birth?
key_questions.looking_for: Constipation dating back to the newborn period

key_questions.question: Is the baby still jaundiced, and how long has the jaundice lasted?
key_questions.looking_for: Prolonged unconjugated jaundice beyond the first two weeks of life

key_questions.question: Does the baby seem cold, and does the baby feel cold to the touch?
Has the baby's cry been hoarse or weak?
Has the baby been growing and gaining weight appropriately?
key_questions.looking_for: Poor weight gain and slow growth

key_questions.question: Did the baby pass meconium in the first 48 hours, and has there been any vomiting or diarrhea?
key_questions.looking_for: Normal meconium passage and absence of vomiting or diarrhea, which argues against obstruction or gastroenteritis

key_questions.question: Did the mother take any antithyroid medication, amiodarone, or receive radioactive iodine during pregnancy?
key_questions.looking_for: Maternal methimazole, propylthiouracil, amiodarone, or radioactive iodine exposure

key_questions.question: Is there any family history of thyroid disease or congenital hypothyroidism?
key_questions.looking_for: Thyroid disease in a parent or sibling, or a sibling with congenital hypothyroidism

key_questions.question: Was the baby born preterm, and was there any iodine exposure such as povidone-iodine or contrast?
key_questions.looking_for: Prematurity or iodine exposure that could cause transient hypothyroidism

key_questions.question: Has the baby had any seizures, breathing difficulty, or episodes of unresponsiveness?
key_questions.looking_for: Seizures, hypoventilation, or obtundation suggesting severe hypothyroidism or another critical illness

reasoning_points: An abnormal newborn screening test with an elevated TSH and low free T4 confirms primary congenital hypothyroidism
Classic presentation includes lethargy, poor feeding, constipation, prolonged jaundice, hypotonia, and a hoarse cry
Exam findings may include a large fontanelle, puffy face, macroglossia, dry skin, umbilical hernia, and delayed relaxation of deep tendon reflexes
Maternal thyroid hormone crosses the placenta, so many infants are asymptomatic at birth and signs appear gradually over the first weeks to months
Distinguish primary (high TSH, low free T4) from central (low or normal TSH, low free T4) hypothyroidism before deciding on imaging
Thyroid ultrasound and scintigraphy determine whether the gland is absent, ectopic, or in place but should not delay treatment
Transient causes such as prematurity, iodine exposure, or maternal antithyroid drugs should be considered because they resolve without lifelong therapy
Treatment with levothyroxine should start as soon as the diagnosis is confirmed, ideally within the first two weeks of life, to protect neurodevelopment

easy: Abnormal newborn screening test with elevated TSH and low free T4
Infant with constipation, prolonged jaundice, poor feeding, and lethargy
Hypotonia with a hoarse cry and puffy face on exam
Large anterior fontanelle and umbilical hernia
medium: Infant with only prolonged jaundice and constipation, otherwise well-appearing
Preterm infant with an abnormal screen where transient hypothyroidism must be excluded
Infant with Down syndrome and hypotonia where hypothyroidism is one of several possibilities
Low free T4 with a low or inappropriately normal TSH suggesting central hypothyroidism
hard: Infant with hypoglycemia, micropenis, or midline defects suggesting congenital hypopituitarism
Infant with vomiting, hyponatremia, and hyperkalemia suggesting congenital adrenal hyperplasia
Infant with an abnormal screen whose mother took antithyroid medication during pregnancy
Infant with severe lethargy, hypothermia, and bradycardia suggesting myxedema
Older infant with growth failure and developmental delay where the diagnosis was missed at birth
